history.content: As an investor what are side effects of Quantitative Easing in US and in EU?

In the US, Quantitative Easing (QE) has generally had a positive effect on stocks, as lower interest rates and easy access to cheap money can improve company profits, which in turn can lead to increased share prices, thus it forces bond yield low.  However, the end of QE and the possibility of interest rate increases can cause negative reactions in the stock market.   In the EU such as Italy, QE has been used to help struggling banks, but it can also lead to the devaluation of the euro, which can impact savers and traders using that currency. Economically, the EU has seen less success with QE when compared to the US and UK, with little to no improvement in unemployment and a risk of falling into another recession.
In the event of mortgage-backed security collapse,   how QE worked out?

Quantitative Easing (QE) was implemented in order to help stabilize the economy during the 2008 financial crisis. In the case of a mortgage-backed security collapse, FED purchased these securities from banks so called  ""Too Big To Fail"" or ""Systemically Important Financial Institution"".  Mortgage rates are heavily influenced by the FED QE program, which holds about $4.5T in mortgage-backed securities and treasuries on the FED's balance sheet. The FED has been holding this balance steady since it ended the QE program a couple years ago, purchasing new securities as old ones mature. This served to increase the demand for these securities, which in turn helped to stabilize their prices and prevent a further decline in the housing market.
what forms of money does the QE come into the market?

The central bank is the Federal Reserve, and is the only entity that is allowed to create money ""out of thin air"". Quantitative Easing (QE) involves the creation of new money by a central bank and their transactions are more about managing the money supply and inflation, ideally trading a bank's paper assets for reserves adding or subtracting to the bank's ability to issue loans.  The increase in bank reserves can then lead to an increase in loans and other forms of credit, helping to boost economic growth.
what do you mean by 'out of thin air'?

When it is said that money is created "out of thin air," it means that the money is being generated by a central authority, such as a central bank, without being backed by any physical commodity like gold or silver. Banks are able to lend and create money out of ""thin air"" by loaning more than they have.   Having a central bank issue money as an economy needs it for trade has been the most successful method to deal with the money created out of thin air, merely serves as IOUs, and it is a good and necessary thing.
The US government debt is over 100% of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP).   The number is calculated using cash accounting and by overestimating inflation.
